owned_invariants: A pattern is written in the syntax of Python's re and matched without regard to case. The module reads that syntax itself, applies the admission rule below, and matches with the regex crate on a pattern it writes from what it read, with every literal as a code point, so the matcher never sees the author's text.

A pattern is admitted when it has one to 256 characters that are not all white space, parses, has no backreference, no repeat inside a repeat, no alternation inside a repeat, every repeat bounded by 64, a product over every repeat of its width and over every alternation of its branches of at most 256, and cannot match the empty string. Each way it fails is its own PATTERN_ code.
The tree is the one Python builds: a common prefix of the branches of an alternation is moved in front of it, and an alternation of single characters or sets is one set.

Syntax Python accepts and this module does not read (anchors and word boundaries, groups other than (...) and (?:...), possessive repeats, octal and named escapes, surrogate escapes and repeat counts beyond the engine's range) is Unread, never guessed. A pattern whose compiled form exceeds 16 MiB is refused as PATTERN_COMPILE_LIMIT.
find gives the leftmost match, the preferred one among those that start there, with its start as a character offset.
boundaries: The classes \w and \s follow the regex crate's Unicode tables, which differ from Python's at a few code points; a reference to a group that does not exist is refused as a backreference where Python calls it a syntax error.
Unread takes precedence over a refusal the rest of the pattern would earn, so the pattern is never partly judged.
Agreement with Python is shown on generated patterns and a hand-written table, not proven.
